segments.text: One of the biggest questions most lab workers ask is,
how do we assess the risk of electrical hazards?
Well, this is quite simple.
Nowadays, lab workers use a procedure
to conduct a thorough risk assessment of electrical hazards.
This involves reviewing the potential hazards
associated with electrical systems or tasks
while assessing the foreseeable risks.
Here are the major steps in risk assessment.
Identify the electrical hazards
related to the task, system, or process.
Specify the electrical work to be performed
within the system or process.
Assess the severity of potential injuries
resulting from the identified electrical hazards.
Identify possible failure modes
that could lead to exposure to electrical hazards
and the potential consequences of such exposure.
And if the risk level is deemed unacceptable,
identify and implement additional measures
or corrective actions.
Now, you remember the hierarchy of controls.
Administrative controls offer a more effective solution
than the use of PPE.
These controls are essential for managing electrical hazards
and ensuring safety in the workplace.
Firstly, proper training ensures that all employees
understand electrical hazards and know how to work safely.
Then, signage helps to alert individuals
to potential hazards
and provide instructions for safe practices.
But most importantly, SOPs outline the standard methods
for performing tasks safely and consistently.
This system of operation covers the step-by-step
procedures for working with or near electrical systems.
Similarly, OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart S
has been a key labor regulation outlining safety practices
for working with electrical equipment.
Unfortunately, many facilities are either not compliant with
or have disregarded this regulation.
Many years back, it was mandatory for anyone who installs,
maintains, repairs, or works near electrical power equipment
to receive training on the associated hazards.
Additionally, the regulation also explicitly bans
previously informal rules,
such as wearing conductive jewelry during electrical tests.
Subpart S has been in effect for several years
and focuses on design safety standards for electrical systems.
These sections apply to individuals who install,
maintain, repair, or work near electrical circuits
or equipment.
Before these updates, many employers followed
the National Fire Protection Association standard
on electrical safety requirements for employee workplaces,
or NFPA 70E, to enhance their electrical safety measures.
In essence, the NFPA standard helped shape
the new OSHA requirements.
Moreover, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics
Engineers, or IEEE, establishes standards to guide
the safe design, operation, and maintenance
of electrical systems and equipment.
This institute provides methodologies
for calculating arc flash hazards
to ensure proper protection
against electrical arc flash incidents.
For electrical test technicians,
being inclined to IEEE standards is needed
for conducting effective tests.
